description: We are 6743V3R, a team of five Informatics Engineering students from the Pontificia Universidad Católica del Perú (PUCP), competing as part of DSC PUCP and Club Blockchain PUCP. We built Drift during the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Together, we worked across data processing, the web viewer, science validation, documentation, and the pitch, with the goal of making SPHEREx data accessible to students, educators, and citizen scientists.
summary: Drift is a public, no-sign-up web viewer that lets anyone look for moving objects in NASA’s SPHEREx survey. Users enter a sky position or an object name and get a short video of real SPHEREx images of that spot, taken on different dates. The tool compares only equivalent infrared colors across dates, flags candidates for human review, and cross-checks them against Gaia DR3 and JPL’s small-body catalog. It targets students, educators and citizen scientists.
details:
Drift shows a sky patch across SPHEREx epochs as a blink animation, with play, step, and speed controls. Users can switch to Difference mode (each epoch minus a reference epoch), Swipe, or Stack; choose one or all six detectors; and change the field of view from 2′ to 20′. Clicking a source shows its 102-band spectrum, and a Data tab lists every image used with its wavelength, release, and flagged pixels.

Images are read from NASA/IPAC IRSA’s SPHEREx collections (spherex_dr1 and spherex_qr3), with pixel data fetched from the public AWS bucket nasa-irsa-spherex. Each frame has its zodiacal background subtracted and flagged pixels removed, then is reprojected to a common grid. Exposures are matched by wavelength, because SPHEREx uses variable linear filters. The candidate detector links detections across dates, fits a linear motion, and cross-matches each result with Gaia DR3 and the JPL Small-Body Identification service. It reports “not cross-matched” when a service does not respond. An injection test adds simulated objects to the real images to measure what fraction the detector recovers.

Drift is built with Python, FastAPI, Astropy, NumPy, SciPy and a vanilla JavaScript front end. It is open source and does not need changes to handle new data releases. Known limitations (6.2″ pixels, about three epochs per location today) are stated in the app and in the README.
